content: Iron and folic acid supplementation has been widely used as a strategy to improve iron stores and prevent anemia in pregnant women. It is also believed to have potential benefits for other maternal and neonatal outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy, either alone or in combination with folic acid or other vitamins and minerals, as part of antenatal care. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search for relevant studies, including randomized and quasi-randomized trials, in multiple databases and registries up to February 2015. They assessed the quality of the trials using Cochrane's standard criteria and employed the GRADE approach to evaluate the quality of evidence for primary outcomes. A random-effects model was used to pool results, given the anticipated variability among trials. A total of 61 trials were included in the analysis, with 44 trials involving 43,274 women contributing data. The findings showed that daily oral iron supplementation significantly reduced the risk of maternal anemia at term by 70% (risk ratio [RR] 0.30; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.46) based on low-quality evidence. It also reduced the risk of iron-deficiency anemia at term (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.69) and iron deficiency at term by 57% (RR 0.43; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.66), though the evidence quality was low. There were no significant differences between the supplementation and control groups in terms of severe anemia during the second or third trimester, maternal infections during pregnancy, maternal mortality, or reported side effects. The evidence for these outcomes was of very low quality. Women who received iron supplementation had higher hemoglobin (Hb) concentrations at term and postpartum but were also at increased risk of having Hb levels above 130 g/L during pregnancy and at term. Iron supplementation was associated with a lower likelihood of delivering low birthweight newborns (8.4% vs. 10.3%; average RR 0.84; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.03) and preterm births (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.03), though these results were not statistically significant. Women taking iron supplements also appeared to deliver slightly heavier babies (mean difference 23.75 g; 95% CI -3.02 to 50.51), but again, the results were not statistically significant. There were no clear differences between groups in neonatal death rates (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.71 to 1.18) or congenital anomalies (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.33). The evidence for these outcomes was of low quality. Among the included studies, 23 were conducted in regions with some malaria risk. Only two of these studies reported malaria-related outcomes, and there was no evidence to suggest that iron supplementation increased the risk of placental malaria. For some outcomes, heterogeneity among the trials exceeded 50%, indicating variability in the results. In conclusion, daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy reduces the risk of maternal anemia and iron deficiency. However, its impact on other maternal and neonatal outcomes is less clear. The effectiveness of this intervention may vary depending on the population's baseline risk of anemia and low birthweight, as well as adherence to the supplementation regimen.
